paragraphs: Taam laamirat pasuq: "vaani tepillati leka Adonai et ratzon" beminchat shabbat - mippene ki bechol beet hammincha hu et tzara shemmitgallin dinim qashim, abal beet minchat shabbat mitgalleh bechinat hakketer haelyon hanniqra ratzon, veal yd kak nikpapim veniknaim haddinim vehaggeburot; velaken niqra atta et ratzon, vekannizkar bedibre rabbenu haari"y za"l beshaar hakkavvanot. veyesh bo od taam, "p happeshat hanneemar bammidrash: amar david lipne hqb"h: ribbono shel olam, en umma zo kishar ummot; ki umot haolam kesheshshotin umishtakkerin, holekin upochazin, vaanachnu lo ken, ella "p sheshshatinu – "vaani tepillati leka Adonai et ratzon", vekannizkar b"lebush".

clarification.explanation: There is a reason for saying the verse "And as for me, may my prayer to You, O Lord, be at a time of favor" specifically at the Sabbath afternoon prayer: on weekdays, the time of Minchah is a time when harsh judgments are revealed (a time of judgment), but on the Sabbath, at the time of Minchah, it is specifically the aspect of the supernal Crown, called "favor," that is revealed, and this force subdues and softens the judgments and severities. For this reason this hour is called "a time of favor." There is another reason, according to the plain sense, brought in the Midrash: King David said before the Holy One, blessed be He, that this nation (Israel) is different from the other nations — for when the nations of the world drink and become drunk they run wild and behave frivolously, but we, even though we have drunk (at the Sabbath meal), still say, "And as for me, may my prayer to You, O Lord, be at a time of favor" — that is, we maintain a serious and dignified attitude toward prayer.
takeaways: According to the esoteric tradition: the Sabbath Minchah is "a time of favor" because the aspect of the Crown, which subdues judgments, is revealed then
According to the plain sense: the verse expresses that Israel maintains a serious attitude toward prayer even after drinking at the Sabbath meal

paragraphs: Pasuq zeh omerim oto achar qedushshat "uba letziyyon"; umi sheddarko lilbosh tallit bemincha, omero achar sheyyilbash. vekatab rabbenu harab shemuel veyittol za"l beseper "chemdat-yisrael": pasuq zeh omer hashlicha tzibbur paam achat, vechozerin haqqahal veomerim oto, vechozer hashlicha tzibbur veomero, vechozerin haqqahal leamero paam shenit; yeuyyan sham. ubeshaar hakkavvanot ubeseper "peri-etz-chayyim" lo nizkar leamero shene peamim; veulay mah shekkatab "chemdat yisrael" ken, lav leikkuba, ella kak haya hamminhag bayyamim hahem; veim kol zeh, kevan denizkar dabar zeh beseper "chemdat yisrael", ulay leikkuba hu; lekak rauy lekol adam leamero shene peamim bezo achar zo, veken ani noheg beezrat Adonai; veomerim pasuq zeh meummad kannizkar b"machaziq beraka". veen mekassim hammetzach vehappanim betallit beminchat shabbat, kemo shekkatab b"shalme-chagiga" beshem mahari"y tzemach za"l.

clarification.explanation: The verse "And as for me, my prayer" is said after the Kedushah of "Uva LeTzion." One who is accustomed to wearing a tallit at Minchah says it after putting on the tallit. Rabbi Shmuel Vital wrote in his book Chemdat Yisrael that the cantor says the verse once, the congregation repeats it, the cantor repeats it again, and the congregation repeats it a second time. Other books (Sha'ar HaKavanot and Pri Etz Chaim) do not mention saying it twice, and it may be that this is only a description of a custom and not a binding obligation. Nevertheless, since it is mentioned in Chemdat Yisrael, it may indeed be a binding obligation — therefore it is proper for every person to say the verse twice in succession, and so the Ben Ish Chai himself is accustomed to do. The verse is said standing. One should not cover the forehead and face with the tallit during the Sabbath Minchah (unlike the custom at other times).
takeaways: It is proper to say the verse "And as for me, my prayer" twice in succession after "Uva LeTzion," while standing
One should not cover the face and forehead with the tallit at the Sabbath Minchah

paragraphs: Motziin seper tora bemincha, veolin shelosha, keneged shelosha rishonot shehem chakema bina daat, veshiba shealu beshacharit hem keneged chesed gebura tiperet netzach hod yesod malkut. vekatabti bsh"q "mqbtzl": kemo shehizhir rabbenu za"l sheyyishtaddel haadam laalot shishshi beshacharit, mippene shehashshishshi hu meulleh yoter shehu bechinat hayyesod, ken yishtaddel laalot bemincha shelishi shehu bedaat, sheggam zeh yoil letiqqun hayyesod, vekaasher tabin min haremez shellahem.

clarification.explanation: At the Sabbath Minchah the Torah scroll is taken out and three people are called up, corresponding to the three supernal sefirot — Chochmah, Binah, and Da'at (unlike the seven called up at the morning service, who correspond to the seven lower sefirot: Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach, Hod, Yesod, Malchut). The Ben Ish Chai writes in his book Makbetzal: just as one should make an effort to receive the sixth aliyah at the morning service (since it corresponds to the sefirah of Yesod, which has a special virtue), so too one should make an effort to receive the third aliyah at Minchah (which corresponds to the sefirah of Da'at), since it too assists in the repair of Yesod — as can be understood from the allusions involved.
takeaways: At the Sabbath Minchah, three people are called up to the Torah, corresponding to Chochmah-Binah-Da'at
One should make an effort to receive specifically the third aliyah at Minchah, just as one makes an effort to receive the sixth aliyah at the morning service

paragraphs: En omerim qaddish achar qeriat seper tora beminchat shabbat, yaan ki beminchat shabbat en mapsiqin b"ashre" ben qeriat seper tora uben qaddish deqodem haamida, laken mehanne qaddish daamida lazeh gam ken vekannizkar b"lebush". veayyen "bet dino shel shelomoh" za"l, simanim ,b,g; yeuyyan sham. upoh bagdad nohagim lomar "mizmor shir leyom hashshabbat" achar qeriat seper tora, veomerim qaddish, umitpallelim amida; veken hamminhag beir haqqodesh yerushalayim ushear artzot hachayyim tvb"b.

clarification.explanation: Kaddish is not said after the Torah reading at the Sabbath Minchah, since at the Sabbath Minchah there is no pause of "Ashrei" between the Torah reading and the Kaddish before the Amidah — and therefore the Kaddish before the Amidah serves this purpose as well. In Baghdad the custom was to say "A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day" after the Torah reading, and then say Kaddish and pray the Amidah — and this is also the custom in Jerusalem and in other lands.
takeaways: There is no separate Kaddish after the Torah reading at the Sabbath Minchah — the Kaddish before the Amidah serves this purpose as well
The custom in Baghdad and Jerusalem: "A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day" is said after the reading, and then Kaddish and the Amidah

paragraphs: Tzarik lehizzaher bitpillat hammincha deshabbat-qodesh harbeh, sheyyesh bah aliyyot gedolot lemala. v"p sheyyesh siddurim shekkatub bahem "umi keammeka yisrael", haiqqar tzarik lomar "keammeka keyisrael", ukemo shekkatab b"shalme-chagiga" beshem mahari"y tzemach b"naggid umetzavveh"; veken hu besiddur rabbenu harasha"sh za"l hannimtza ittanu. umilleshon shaar-hakkavvanot shehizkir "keammeka yisrael", en mizzeh hokacha kelal. veamarti bs"d, degirsa shel "keyisrael" hi nekona yoter, yaan ki bishmuel-b', siman z', ketib "keyisrael", ubedibre hayyamim, siman y"z, ketib "yisrael", laken nireh deshappir katab mahari"y tzemach za"l dtz"l "keyisrael", mishshum dezehu pasuq dinbiim. vekayyotze bazeh matzinu baamirat "migdol yeshuot malko" bebirkat hammazon, dibshabbat omerim "migdol" kemo shenneemar bannebiim (shemuel b kb,n), ubechol "magdil" kemo shenneemar biktubim (tehillim ych,k).

clarification.explanation: One must be very careful in the Sabbath Minchah prayer, since it involves great spiritual ascents. Regarding the wording of the prayer, some prayer books have "and who is like Your people Israel" (umi ke'amcha Yisrael), but the essential text is "like Your people, like Israel" (ke'amcha keYisrael) — as several kabbalists have written, and as appears in the prayer book of the Rashash. The Ben Ish Chai adds and reinforces this: since in the book of Samuel II it is written "keYisrael" (with the letter kaf), whereas in Chronicles it is written "Yisrael" (without the kaf), the wording "keYisrael" should be preferred, since the original verse is from the Prophets (Samuel) and not from the Writings (Chronicles). A similar example: in saying "Magdol yeshu'ot malko" (Tower of salvation to His king) in Grace After Meals, on the Sabbath one says "Magdol" (as it is said in the book of Samuel, which is from the Prophets), while on weekdays one says "Magdil" (as it is said in Psalms, which is from the Writings).
takeaways: The wording of the prayer should be "like Your people, like Israel," not "and who is like Your people Israel"
Wordings based on verses from the Prophets should be preferred over parallel wordings from the Writings

paragraphs: Mah sheomerim baamida: "yakkiru baneka veyedeu ki meitteka hi menuchatam", tzarik lekavven betebat "meitteka": meet k' shehu keter – menuchatam, ki beminchat shabbat nimshak heara min hakketer, velaken anachnu omerim atta "yakkiru baneka" shehem yisrael, veyedeu ki meet k', shehi hakketer, mishsham nimshak lahem menuchatam atta beshaa zo, vekamporash bedibre haari"y za"l beshaar hakkavvanot.

clarification.explanation: When saying, in the Amidah, "Your children shall recognize and know that their rest comes from You," one should intend, in the word "me'itcha" ("from You"), the division "me'et kaf" — the letter kaf alluding to the sefirah of Keter (Crown). The intention is: at the Sabbath Minchah, an illumination is drawn to us from the aspect of Keter, and therefore it is said, "Your children shall recognize" (that is, the people of Israel) so that they know that it is specifically from the aspect of Keter ("me'et kaf") that their rest is drawn to them at this hour — as is explained in the words of the holy Ari in Sha'ar HaKavanot.
takeaways: When saying "me'itcha" in the Sabbath Minchah prayer, one should intend the division "me'et kaf" — an allusion to the sefirah of Keter

paragraphs: Beamero "veal menuchatam yaqdishu et shemeka" yekavven limsor napsho al qiddush hashshem; veyesh sod gadol bedabar zeh, sheyyesh tzorek gadol atta bimsirat nepesh al qiddush hashshem, vekamporash beshaar-hakkavvanot.

clarification.explanation: When saying, further in the prayer, "and through their rest they shall sanctify Your name," one should intend and devote one's soul to the sanctification of God's name. There is a great secret in this matter — for it is specifically at this hour that there is a special and great need for self-sacrifice for the sanctification of God's name, as is explained in the words of the holy Ari in Sha'ar HaKavanot.
takeaways: One should intend, when saying "and through their rest they shall sanctify Your name," a devotion of the soul to the sanctification of God's name

paragraphs: Inyan haqqedushsha shel chazarat tepillat mincha deshabbat, yesh bah sod gadol, ki atta haqqedushsha hazzot nimsheket mimmaqom elyon vegabohha meod ukemo shekkatab rabbenu za"l beshaar-hakkavvanot, al-ken tzarik lehizzaher bah meod bekavvanatah.

clarification.explanation: Regarding the Kedushah said in the leader's repetition at the Sabbath Minchah — it contains a great secret, since this Kedushah is drawn from a very supernal and high place, as the holy Ari wrote in Sha'ar HaKavanot. For this reason one must be very careful and concentrate one's intention when reciting it.
takeaways: One should concentrate and focus well when reciting the Kedushah in the repetition of the prayer at the Sabbath Minchah, since it is drawn from a specially supernal source

paragraphs: Inyan shelosh peamim "tzidqateka veku'" - lepi happeshat omerim otah bemincha shel shabbat keneged shelosha tzaddiqim: yosep hatztzaddiq alayv hashshalom, umosheh rabbenu alayv hashshalom, vedavid hammelek alayv hashshalom, shennipteru beshabbat; ak taam iqqere "p hassod hu, ki tzerikin anachnu atta leorer "y nishmot shelosha tzaddiqim hannizkarim, tiqqun gadol hatztzarik leet-atta beminchat shabbat, ki leet-atta tzerika hammalkut lehaalot orot miyyayin nuqbin lemaqom elyon vegabohha, utzerika lishlosha neshamot shel shelosha tzaddiqim hannizkarim, sheyyaalu gam hem orot miyyayin nuqbin immah. veim chal shabbat berosh chodesh, enah tzerika hammalkut el aliyyat hashshelosha tzaddiqim hannizkarim sheyyihyu maalim immah, velaken en omerim shelosh peamim "tzidqateka tzedeq" hannizkar beshabbat shechal berosh chodesh, vekannizkar bedibre rabbenu haari"y za"l beshaar-hakkavvanot. vehamminhag pashut degam keshechal shabbat beyom tob vachanukka ushear yamim sheen omerim bahem techinna bechol, deen omerim "tzidqateka tzedeq"; velo od, ella gam im ellu yamim sheen omerim bahem techinna beyom rishon beshabbat, name en omerim "tzidqateka tzedeq" beyom shabbat. veal zeh en beyadenu taam leda ek naaleh beoto shabbat hattiqqun hannizkar hatztzarik lammalkut "y shelosha tzaddiqim baamirat shelosh peamim hannizkarim. veayyen "emet leyaaqob" ninayv za"l, dap q"b, ammud d, siman yo"d. vekatab li harab haggaon morenu rabbi eliyyahu minni nr"v, shemmatza biktibat yad shel harab yr" za"l veza"l: minhag qadum b"bet-el" ykb"tz lekavven kol hakkavvanot beleb ben hachazara leqaddish, veken hu baamirat "tzidqateka tzedeq" mekavvenim hakkavvanot hannizkarot bemachashaba, chutz merosh chodesh sheen mekavvenim shum kavvana ben hachazara leqaddish; ad kan leshon harab hyr" za"l.

clarification.explanation: The verse "Tzidkatcha tzedek" ("Your righteousness is everlasting righteousness") is said three times in the Sabbath Minchah prayer. According to the plain sense, this corresponds to three righteous men who passed away on the Sabbath: Joseph the Righteous, Moses our Teacher, and King David. But the primary reason is according to the esoteric tradition: it is necessary to arouse, through the souls of these three righteous men, a great repair needed specifically at the Sabbath Minchah — for at this hour the sefirah of Malchut must raise "lights of feminine waters" (illuminations rising from below to above) to a supernal and high place, and this is accomplished with the help of the souls of the three righteous men. But when the Sabbath falls on Rosh Chodesh, Malchut does not need the ascent of the three righteous men to the same degree, and therefore on that Sabbath the three recitations of "Tzidkatcha tzedek" are not said. This is also the widespread custom: when the Sabbath falls on a festival, on Chanukah, and on any day on which Tachanun is not said during the week — "Tzidkatcha tzedek" is not said; and likewise when the following Sunday is not a day on which Tachanun is said, "Tzidkatcha tzedek" is also not said on that Sabbath. The Ben Ish Chai notes that he has no clear reason for how the repair needed for Malchut is then achieved through the three righteous men, and brings in the name of Rabbi Eliyahu Mani an ancient custom in "Beit El" to direct all the inner intentions in one's heart between the repetition and the Kaddish, including at the saying of "Tzidkatcha tzedek," except on Rosh Chodesh, when no special intention is directed there.
takeaways: "Tzidkatcha tzedek" is said three times at a regular Sabbath Minchah, but not when the Sabbath falls on Rosh Chodesh, a festival, Chanukah, or any day without Tachanun
According to the esoteric tradition, this recitation arouses a supernal repair through the souls of Joseph the Righteous, Moses, and King David

paragraphs: Bisudat hammincha, qodem shettittol yadeka l"hammotzi", tomar beqol ram ubesimcha rabba: "atqinu saoteda demehemanuta shelimetta chedveta demalka qaddisha, atqinu seudeta demalka, da hi seudeta dizer anpin", vekannizkar beshaar-hakkavvanot. veda ki shamati shehachasidim hamqubbalim beir haqqodesh tvb"b en omerim "zeer anpin" beperush, ella omerim z" berashe tebot davqa - hen belimmudam beqabbala, hen b"atqinu veku'" hannizkar; veqashya li al dibrehem mippiyyut "bene hekela diksippin" shettiqqenu rabbenu haari"y za"l, umishsham reaya dehaya omer "zeer anpin" beperush, lehashlim hammishqal; veen lomar derabbenu haari"y za"l shane, deadderabba, lihyoto gadol meod, dibburo poel yoter, veit leh lemechash tepe mishshear adam. ubeseper "keter malkut" ita vezeh leshono: lihyot shehashshaa hazzot ha"zeer anpin" ola baaliyya gedola ad haddiqna, en min harauy shennazkir oto betoar zeh shel "zeer anpin", laken leet-atta yomru "zehir anpin"; ad kan debarayv. vaani noheg lesayyem: "da hi seudeta demalka qaddisha" bilbad, velipamim ani mesayyem: "da hi seudeta demalka qaddisha zeer anpin".

clarification.explanation: At the meal of Minchah (the third Sabbath meal), before washing the hands for the blessing of Hamotzi, one should say aloud and with great joy a short Aramaic formula beginning "Atkinu se'udata dimheimenuta shelemata" — meaning the preparation of the meal in honor of the completeness of faith and the joy of the holy King, the meal of "Ze'ir Anpin" (a kabbalistic term). The Ben Ish Chai mentions that he heard that the kabbalist pietists in Jerusalem do not say the expression "Ze'ir Anpin" explicitly, but only its initials ("Za"), both in the study of Kabbalah and in this formula — but he raises a difficulty from the poem "Benei heichala dichsifin" of the holy Ari, in which "Ze'ir Anpin" is indeed said explicitly in order to complete the meter of the poem, from which it follows that the Ari himself did not refrain from saying it explicitly. There is a book (Keter Malchut) that gives another reason for refraining from saying "Ze'ir Anpin" at that hour — because at that time it ascends to a very high level (up to the "Dikna," the Beard, a term for a supernal degree), and therefore it is proper to call it by another name, "Zahir Anpin." The Ben Ish Chai relates that he himself is accustomed to end the formula with the words "Da hi se'udata demalka kadisha" alone, and sometimes adds "Ze'ir Anpin" as well.
takeaways: Before the blessing of Hamotzi at the third meal, one says aloud the formula "Atkinu se'udata"
There are various customs regarding saying "Ze'ir Anpin" explicitly or by its initials — the Ben Ish Chai did not rule decisively and practiced with flexibility

paragraphs: En bechinat qiddush al hayyayin bisuda zo, lepi sheshshoresh seuda zo hu bemaqom elyon vegabohha meod, sheen sham bechinat yayin shehu din ugebura; veim kol zeh, beemtza akilat hasseuda hazzo tzarik lishtot yayin ulebarek alayv "bore peri haggapen", abal lo leqaddesh alayv biqdushshat hayyom bitchillat hasseuda kebishar hasseudot, ukemo shekkatab kol zeh beshaar-hakkavvanot, dap q"y; yeuyyan sham. vbsh"q "mqbtzl" nistappaqti, im en lo ella kos echad bilbad mah yaaseh? im yishtehu betok hasseuda vibarek "birkat hammazon" belo kos, o adip tepe lebarek birkat hammazon al hakkos, velo yishteh betok hasseuda. veheeleti deadip tepe lehannicho lebirkat hammazon; veap al gab demitzvot kos zeh shel tok hasseuda, zemannah qodem kos birkat-hammazon kevan demitzvot kos birkat-hammazon adipa mimmetzuvva zo - nidchet mippaneha. vehebeti bs"d reaya lazeh miggemara deyoma, dap l"d, biplugta detanna-qamma verabbi, dekatebu hattosapot: ikka benayhu, tzibbur shello haya lahem nesakim ella leechad veku', dilpi zeh nimtza, lemaen deamar "gemar shel arbit mishshel shacharit", "g deatta, shel arbit hi lepanenu ubeyadenu, im kol zeh en maqribin hannesakim atta, ella mashhim otam ad shacharit mishshum deadip tepe; veken hainyan lemaen deamar hashsheni; velaken gam beniddon didan, "p shehu yosheb betok hasseuda, umetzuvveh zo dishtiyyat hakkos lepanayv - mannicha hakkos lebirkat hammazon mishshum deadip tepe.

clarification.explanation: One does not recite Kiddush over wine at the third meal, since the source of this meal is in a very supernal and high place that has no aspect of wine at all (which symbolizes judgment and severity). Nevertheless, in the middle of eating this meal there is an obligation to drink wine and recite the blessing "Who creates the fruit of the vine" over it — but not as a Kiddush at the beginning of the meal as in the other two meals. The Ben Ish Chai discusses the case where there is only one cup of wine: should it be drunk during the meal and Grace After Meals recited without a cup, or is it preferable to save it for Grace After Meals and not drink during the meal? He rules that it is preferable to leave the cup for Grace After Meals, even though the commandment of drinking the cup in the middle of the meal comes first in time — because the commandment of the cup at Grace After Meals is more important and takes precedence over it. He brings proof for this from a discussion in the Talmud, tractate Yoma, regarding the offering of libations in the Holy Temple, where too something earlier in time is sometimes deferred for something more important that will come afterward.
takeaways: There is no Kiddush over wine at the third meal, but there is an obligation to drink wine and recite a blessing over it during the meal
One who has only one cup of wine should preferably save it for Grace After Meals rather than drink it during the meal

paragraphs: Betok hasseuda tzarik lehabi shette aguddot hahadas utebarek vetaricha bahem, ukemo shekkatab beshaar-hakkavvanot. venireh li detzarik lomar gam ken "zakor veshamor bedibbur echad neemru" kemo beshacharit. veen minhagenu lehaqqip hashshulchan beminchat shabbat, yaan ki lo nitparesh dabar zeh bedibre rabbenu haari"y za"l al seuda zo, ak vadday tzarik lehannicha y"b kikkarot kepi hassod, kemo seudat hallayla veshacharit; vegam tzarik shene mappot, achat lemala min hallechem veachat lematta; deap al gab debisuda zo lekka qiddush, ubatel taam boshet happat - ha ita od shene teamim deshayeki gam bisuda zo. ubeinyan netilat yadayim yaaseh kemo shekkatabnu leel. vekatab beseper "bene yissashkar" sheyyesh qabbala beyadam lomar bisuda shelishit shelosha peamim mizmor "Adonai roe".

clarification.explanation: During the third meal, two bundles of myrtle should be brought, a blessing recited over them, and they should be smelled, as the holy Ari wrote. The Ben Ish Chai adds that one should also say the phrase "Remember and Observe were said in a single utterance," as is said at the morning meal. There is no custom of circling the table (as is done at the other meals) at the third meal, since this was not explained in the words of the Ari regarding this meal. Nevertheless, twelve loaves of bread should still be placed (according to the esoteric tradition), as at the night and morning meals, and two cloths should be placed — one over the bread and one beneath it — even though at this meal there is no Kiddush and no reason of "the shame of the bread" (hiding the bread because the wine precedes it), since there are two other reasons that apply to this meal as well. The washing of the hands is done as explained in the previous halachot. The Benei Yissaschar wrote that there is a tradition to say, at the third meal, the psalm "The Lord is my shepherd" (Psalm 23) three times.
takeaways: At the third meal, a blessing is recited over two bundles of myrtle and they are smelled, and "Remember and Observe were said in a single utterance" is said
Twelve loaves and two cloths are placed as at the other meals, but there is no circling of the table
There is a custom to say the psalm "The Lord is my shepherd" three times at the third meal

paragraphs: Echad haish veechad haishsha chayyabin leqayyem seuda shelishit bepat veal hashshulchan kisuda rishona usheniyya been hepresh; vaapillu chal yom tob lihyot bemotzae-shabbat, gam ken tzarik leqayyem seuda shelishit bepat. veyizzaharu lomar tepillat "yehe raava" qodem sheyyittol yadayv lisuda zo. vehappiyyut shel "bene hekela diksippin" shessidder rabbenu haari"y za"l lisuda zo, shamati sheyyesh chasidim nimnaim leamero mechamat happachad, shennizkar bo debarim keneged haqqelippot, veomerim sheyyereim lehitgarot baqqelippot. verabbenu haari"y za"l, hamchabber happiyyut shane, derab cheleh. venireh li dehannoheg leamero lo yebattel minhago, veraq yizzaher lomar min pasuq "qeribu li veku'" belachash mammash, ad pasuq "ari hashta", ukesheyyatchil bappasuq "ari hashta" yagbihha qolo, vehake adip veen bazeh mechosh; vaanachnu en nohagim leamero kelal.

clarification.explanation: Both men and women are obligated to hold the third meal with bread and at a table, no differently from the first and second meals. Even when a festival falls on the night following the Sabbath, one is still obligated to hold the third meal with bread. One should be careful to say the prayer "Yehei ra'ava" before washing the hands for this meal. Regarding the poem "Benei heichala dichsifin," which the holy Ari composed for the third meal — the Ben Ish Chai heard that there are pietists who refrain from saying it because it contains references to the forces of impurity (kelipot), and they are concerned about "provoking" them. But he explains that the holy Ari, who composed the poem, possessed great spiritual power ("rav cheilei") and could handle this, and therefore one who is accustomed to saying it need not abandon his custom — he need only be careful to say the passage from "Karivu li" to "Ari hashta" in a genuine whisper, and when he reaches "Ari hashta" he should raise his voice — this is preferable, and there is no concern in doing so. Nevertheless, the Ben Ish Chai notes that they themselves (in his family) are not accustomed to say it at all.
takeaways: The third meal with bread is obligatory for both men and women, even when a festival falls on the night after the Sabbath
"Yehei ra'ava" is said before this meal

Regarding the poem "Benei heichala dichsifin": one who is accustomed to saying it should say part of it in a whisper (from "Karivu li" to "Ari hashta"), though the Ben Ish Chai's own family did not say it at all

paragraphs: Zeman seuda shelishit achar tepillat hammincha; veim neenas vaasaah miqqodem, yatza bediabad, ubilbad shello yaasenna qodem shesh shaot umechetza, deaz hi biklal shacharit. ulepi hassod sheggilla rabbenu haari"y bazeh nireh, deim asaah qodem tepillat mincha, lo yatza yede chobato gam bediabad.

clarification.explanation: The time for the third meal is after the Minchah prayer. One who was prevented by circumstances and held it before the Minchah prayer has fulfilled his obligation after the fact, provided he did not hold it before six and a half hours (seasonal, according to the day's division into hours), since before that time it is still considered part of the morning meal and not a separate third meal. But according to the esoteric tradition revealed by the holy Ari, it appears that if one held the third meal before the Minchah prayer, he has not fulfilled his obligation at all, even after the fact.
takeaways: The time for the third meal is after the Minchah prayer, and not before six and a half hours (relative to the day)
According to the esoteric tradition, if the meal was held before the Minchah prayer, the obligation is not fulfilled at all, even after the fact
